summary:
Visitors in the Comunitat Valenciana stand under two layers of law. The national layer is Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023, which guarantees real and effective equality for trans persons and LGTBI rights: under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative route that replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, and the law regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16. With administrative self-declaration, Spain stands alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules. A visitor whose documents reflect a self-declared gender is treated on that basis in public facilities throughout the community.

Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months; both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so a gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence. Courts are applying the aggravation in practice: in Vigo, a Tribunal de Instancia used the transfobia aggravation for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300.

The Comunitat Valenciana holds a dedicated integral law on the right to gender identity and expression and a general LGTBI-equality statute, one of only a small number of communities to legislate in both categories. Ley 8/2017, de 7 de abril, integral del reconocimiento del derecho a la identidad y a la expresión de género (BOE-A-2017-5118) makes its purpose the guarantee of an adequate normative framework for gender self-determination for people whose felt gender identity differs from that assigned at birth, and requires public bodies of the Comunitat Valenciana to treat people according to their felt gender identity. Ley 23/2018, de 29 de noviembre, de igualdad de las personas LGTBI (BOE-A-2019-281) covers non-discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity and expression, with access and admission rights at Article 56.

Enforcement evidence in the community is documented. The Audiencia Provincial de Valencia, Section 5, handled a case arising from a June 2022 incident in a Valencia park in the Patraix district, where an 18-year-old with several minors insulted, chased, recorded and mocked a trans woman solely because of her gender identity. The adult accepted six months' prison, suspended on condition of committing no offence for two years, plus a EUR 720 fine and a EUR 1,000 moral-damages indemnity to the victim; two minors had already been sentenced to supervision measures, and the case was handled by the fiscal coordinadora de delitos de odio. The same pattern of a gender-identity-motivated offence investigated, charged and resulting in a court sentence also appears in the national picture, where a juvenile gang in Valencia that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, with two minors judged separately.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have applied across Spain since 2005, and Spain is recognised in comparative rankings as among the most LGBT-friendly countries.
tangentialFactors:
The Comunitat Valenciana's statutory framework is unusual in structure rather than in direction: the Spanish trans-rights platform plataformatrans.es lists it with two statutes, Ley 8/2017 and Ley 23/2018, while other communities in the same inventory carry a single statute, among them Cataluña with Ley 11/2014 and Aragón with Ley 4/2018. The dual structure has not been narrowed by later amendment.

A 2025 radiography of public educational policies published by the LGTBI federation places the Comunidad Valenciana with Madrid, Extremadura, Murcia and Navarra among the leaders on educational policy coverage, and records that the Valencian parliament completed its gender legislation. This bears on schools and youth programming rather than on visitor-facing rules, but it indicates the political direction of the community's institutions.

Ley 4/2023 did reform the offences against sexual freedom at Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis of the Criminal Code, which is the statutory route through which much of the protection relevant to visitors actually reaches a courtroom.
localsOnly:
Residents of the Comunitat Valenciana deal with two administrative regimes. Title III of Ley 8/2017 provides for administrative documentation and an advice-and-support service for trans people and their families, and Article 1 obliges public bodies of the community to treat people according to their felt gender identity. Rectification of the gender mention itself is handled directly before the Civil Registry under Article 43 of Ley 4/2023 from age 16, without diagnosis or treatment history.

Ley 23/2018 carries an enforcement machinery that residents can invoke: Article 56 covers access and admission, Article 57 reverses the burden of proof in discrimination proceedings, and Title V, Articles 58 to 66, establishes a regime of administrative infringements and sanctions for discrimination against LGTBI people.

For minors, Ley 4/2023 regulates consent for medical procedures between ages 12 and 16 and permits recognition of gender identity from age 12 under conditions, which governs school and health settings for resident families.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the inventory contains no sourced account of how the suspension condition in the Valencia sentence was monitored, and no data on reporting rates for gender-identity-motivated offences in the community, so the single documented conviction cannot be read as a measure of how often such incidents are reported or prosecuted.

Unresolved: no source in the inventory states whether Ley 8/2017 or Ley 23/2018 has been amended, narrowed or partially repealed since Ley 4/2023 entered into force, nor whether any provision of either statute conflicts with the national framework. The claim that the community has not amended its provisions rests on the trans-rights platform's inventory and is not independently confirmed against the current consolidated texts.

Not sourced: the inventory carries no material on healthcare access for trans visitors, on the practical availability of the advice-and-support service under Title III of Ley 8/2017, or on how facility access rules are applied in practice in hotels, spas and other venues a visitor would use.

Not sourced: no evidence in the inventory addresses hate-crime outcomes under Ley 23/2018's administrative sanctions regime, so the enforcement picture rests on criminal proceedings alone.
